text: INJUSTICE, n. A burden which of all those that we load upon others and carry ourselves is lightest in the hands and heaviest upon the back.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: VOTE, n. The instrument and symbol of a freeman's power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1948), p. 359. Originally published in 1906 as The Cynic's Word Book.

text: DECIDE, v.i. To succumb to the preponderance of one set of influences over another set.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: APPEAL, v.t. In law, to put the dice into the box for another throw.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: COMMERCE, n. A kind of transaction in which A plunders from B the goods of C, and for compensation B picks the pocket of D of money belonging to E.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: MONARCH, n. A person engaged in reigning. Formerly the monarch ruled, as the derivation of the word attests, and as many subjects have had occasion to learn. In Russia and the Orient the monarch has still a considerable influence in public affairs and in the disposition of the human head, but in western Europe political administration is mostly entrusted to his ministers, he being somewhat preoccupied with reflections relating to the status of his own head.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: Government by kings was first introduced into the world by the Heathens, from whom the children of Israel copied the custom. It was the most prosperous invention the Devil ever set on foot for the promotion of idolatry.
locator: Thomas Paine, Common Sense (1776)

text: APPLAUSE, n. The echo of a platitude.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: Truth gains more even by the errors of one who, with due study and preparation, thinks for himself, than by the true opinions of those who only hold them because they do not suffer themselves to think.
locator: J. S. Mill, On Liberty (1895), Chapter 2, p. 63

text: RAILROAD, n. The chief of many mechanical devices enabling us to get away from where we are to where we are no better off. For this purpose the railroad is held in highest favor by the optimist, for it permits him to make the transit with great expedition.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: ACCIDENT, n. An inevitable occurrence due to the action of immutable natural laws.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: GHOST, n. The outward and visible sign of an inward fear.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: Accounting for the uncommon behavior of ghosts, Heine mentions somebody's ingenious theory to the effect that they are as much afraid of us as we of them. Not quite, if I may judge from such tables of comparative speed as I am able to compile from memories of my own experience.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: APPETITE, n. An instinct thoughtfully implanted by Providence as a solution to the labor question.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: EXILE, n. One who serves his country by residing abroad, yet is not an ambassador.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: BABE or BABY, n. A misshapen creature of no particular age, sex, or condition, chiefly remarkable for the violence of the sympathies and antipathies it excites in others, itself without sentiment or emotion. There have been famous babes; for example, little Moses, from whose adventure in the bulrushes the Egyptian hierophants of seven centuries before doubtless derived their idle tale of the child Osiris being preserved on a floating lotus leaf.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: BEG, v. To ask for something with an earnestness proportioned to the belief that it will not be given.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: BEGGAR, n. One who has relied on the assistance of his friends.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: BENEFACTOR, n. One who makes heavy purchases of ingratitude, without, however, materially affecting the price, which is still within the means of all.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: BORE, n. A person who talks when you wish him to listen.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: DEFAME, v.t. To lie about another. To tell the truth about another.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, "Decalogue", The Devil's Dictionary (1906).

text: COMFORT, n. A state of mind produced by contemplation of a neighbor's uneasiness.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: COWARD, n. One who in a perilous emergency thinks with his legs.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: DARING, n. One of the most conspicuous qualities of a man in security.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: END, n. The position farthest removed on either hand from the Interlocutor.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: GOOSE, n. A bird that supplies quills for writing. These, by some occult process of nature, are penetrated and suffused with various degrees of the bird's intellectual energies and emotional character, so that when inked and drawn mechanically across paper by a person called an "author," there results a very fair and accurate transcript of the fowl's thought and feeling. The difference in geese, as discovered by this ingenious method, is considerable: many are found to have only trivial and insignificant powers, but some are seen to be very great geese indeed.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: GRAVE, n. A place in which the dead are laid to await the coming of the medical student.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: HOSPITALITY, n. The virtue which induces us to feed and lodge certain persons who are not in need of food and lodging.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: He who lets the world, or his own portion of it, choose his plan of life for him, has no need of any other faculty than the ape-like one of imitation. He who chooses his plan for himself, employs all his faculties.
locator: J.S. Mill, On Liberty (Henry Holt, New York: 1895), Chapter 3, p. 106.

text: MARTYR, n. One who moves along the line of least reluctance to a desired death.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: MISFORTUNE, n. The kind of fortune that never misses.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: YEAR, n. A period of three hundred and sixty-five disappointments.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: ORATORY, n. A conspiracy between speech and action to cheat the understanding. A tyranny tempered by stenography.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: REFORM, v. A thing that mostly satisfies reformers opposed to reformation.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: DISCUSSION, n. A method of confirming others in their errors.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: TRIAL, n. A formal inquiry designed to prove and put upon record the blameless characters of judges, advocates and jurors. In order to effect this purpose it is necessary to supply a contrast in the person of one who is called the defendant, the prisoner, or the accused. If the contrast is made sufficiently clear this person is made to undergo such an affliction as will give the virtuous gentlemen a comfortable sense of their immunity, added to that of their worth.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: WIT, n. The salt with which the American humorist spoils his intellectual cookery by leaving it out.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: WITTICISM, n. A sharp and clever remark, usually quoted, and seldom noted; what the Philistine is pleased to call a "joke."
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: We have it in our power to begin the world over again.
locator: Thomas Paine, "Common Sense" (1776), conclusion; in Philip S. Foner, ed., The Complete Writings of Thomas Paine (1945), vol. 1, p. 45. Quoted by President Ronald Reagan in a televised presidential campaign debate with Walter F. Mondale (October 7, 1984).

text: ABILITY, n. The natural equipment to accomplish some small part of the meaner ambitions distinguishing able men from dead ones. In the last analysis ability is commonly found to consist mainly in a high degree of solemnity. Perhaps, however, this impressive quality is rightly appraised; it is no easy task to be solemn.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: ABSENT, adj. Peculiarly exposed to the tooth of detraction; vilifed; hopelessly in the wrong; superseded in the consideration and affection of another.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: I always pass on good advice. It is the only thing to do with it. It is never of any use to oneself.
locator: Oscar Wilde, An Ideal Husband (1895), Act I.

text: AFFLICTION, n. An acclimatizing process preparing the soul for another and bitter world.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: AGE, n. That period of life in which we compound for the vices that we still cherish by reviling those that we have no longer the enterprise to commit.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: ARCHITECT, n. One who drafts a plan of your house, and plans a draft of your money.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: FIDELITY, n. A virtue peculiar to those who are about to be betrayed.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: Things are pretty, graceful, rich, elegant, handsome, but, until they speak to the imagination, not yet beautiful.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, "Beauty", The Conduct of Life (1860)

text: Do not craze yourself with thinking, but go about your business anywhere.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803-1882), U.S. essayist, poet, philosopher. 'Experience', Essays, Second Series (1844).

text: CAT, n. A soft, indestructible automaton provided by nature to be kicked when things go wrong in the domestic circle.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: It is immoral to use private property in order to alleviate the horrible evils that result from the institution of private property.
locator: Oscar Wilde, “The Soul of Man Under Socialism,” Complete Works (New York: 1989), p. 1079, ¶ 5

text: CONTEMPT, n. The feeling of a prudent man for an enemy who is too formidable safely to be opposed.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: A great part of courage is the courage of having done the thing before.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, "Culture," The Conduct of Life (1860).

text: CRITIC, n. A person who boasts himself hard to please because nobody tries to please him.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: Those who are esteemed umpires of taste are often persons who have acquired some knowledge of admired pictures or sculptures, and have an inclination for whatever is elegant; but if you inquire whether they are beautiful souls, and whether their own acts are like fair pictures, you learn that they are selfish and sensual.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, “The Poet,” Essays, Second Series (1883), p. 9

text: CURIOSITY, n. An objectionable quality of the female mind. The desire to know whether or not a woman is cursed with curiosity is one of the most active and insatiable passions of the masculine soul.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: DANCE, v.i. To leap about to the sound of tittering music, preferably with arms about your neighbor's wife or daughter. There are many kinds of dances, but all those requiring the participation of the two sexes have two characteristics in common: they are conspicuously innocent, and warmly loved by the vicious.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: DENTIST, n. A prestidigitator who, putting metal into your mouth, pulls coins out of your pocket.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: Dreams are the touchstones of our characters.
locator: Henry David Thoreau, in "A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers" (1849).

text: DUTY, n. That which sternly impels us in the direction of profit, along the line of desire.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: ECONOMY, n. Purchasing the barrel of whiskey that you do not need for the price of the cow that you cannot afford.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: EDUCATION, n. That which discloses to the wise and disguises from the foolish their lack of understanding.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: We live in the age of the overworked, and the under-educated; the age in which people are so industrious that they become absolutely stupid.
locator: Oscar Wilde, Gilbert, in The Critic as Artist, pt. 2, Intentions (1891)

text: EPITAPH, n. An inscription on a tomb, showing that virtues acquired by death have a retroactive effect.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: FAMOUS, adj. Conspicuously miserable.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).
